title: Capsule Staining

references.label: General microbiology/molecular biology laboratory manuals (ASM curriculum resources)

purpose: To visualize the polysaccharide (or, in some species, polypeptide) capsule surrounding certain bacterial cells, which does not take up most standard stains and is otherwise invisible by simple or Gram staining.
principle: Bacterial capsules are largely non-ionic and resist most standard dyes, so capsule staining methods typically rely on staining the cell body and the background separately while leaving the capsule itself unstained, producing a clear halo around the cell against a contrasting background — a negative-staining approach rather than direct staining of the capsule material.
requiredReagents: Background stain (e.g. an acidic dye such as Congo red or nigrosin, depending on method)
Cell body counterstain (e.g. crystal violet, depending on method)

procedure.instruction: Mix a loopful of the bacterial culture with the background stain directly on a slide, without heat-fixing (heat fixation can shrink or distort the capsule).
Spread the mixture into a thin film and air-dry without heat.
Apply the cell body counterstain per the specific method's timing, then gently rinse and blot dry.
Examine under oil immersion, looking for a clear, unstained halo (the capsule) surrounding stained cell bodies against the stained/contrasting background.

observations: A distinct, clear zone (the capsule) surrounding stained bacterial cells against a darker, stained background.
interpretation: Presence of a clear halo indicates a capsule-producing organism under the growth conditions tested; capsule expression can vary with growth conditions (e.g. specific media or growth phase), so a negative result under one set of conditions does not necessarily rule out capsule production under different conditions.
criticalNotes: Avoid heat-fixing the smear — capsules are delicate and can shrink, distort, or be destroyed by heat, producing a false negative appearance.
precautions: Follow standard aseptic technique when preparing the smear from a live culture.
Handle background/counterstain dyes per their safety data sheets.
biosafetyNotes: Handle the source culture per its specific biosafety risk assessment, since capsule-forming organisms often include recognized pathogens.
limitations: Capsule expression is frequently condition-dependent, so results should be interpreted alongside knowledge of the growth conditions used, not treated as a fixed, unconditional species trait.
This method visualizes the capsule as a halo but does not itself confirm its chemical composition.
